canberra.title: The End of Oak Street is the dinosaur flick audiences have been waiting 33 years for
canberra.snippet: Jurassic Park set a standard for dinosaur blockbusters that hasn’t been topped since its release 33 years ago. For some reason or a...
canberra.content:
The End of Oak Street brings back dinosaurs to the big screen in a fun mystery and an awesome cast. Photo: Warner Bros Pictures.

Jurassic Park set a standard for dinosaur blockbusters that hasn’t been topped since its release 33 years ago.

For some reason or another, dinosaur movies struggle to deliver the fantasy and awe that come with the creatures they depict, so much so that even sequels in the Jurassic Park franchise have tried and failed to live up to that first film.

So it gives me great pleasure to report that The End of Oak Street is the best movie to feature the prehistoric beasts since the 1993 classic.

The End of Oak Street follows the Platt Family in the early 1980s. Greg (Ewan McGregor) and Denise (Anne Hathaway) deal with the challenges that come with being parents to their teenagers Audrey (Maisy Stella) and Brian (Christian Convery).

On what appears to be another mundane morning, the entirety of Oak Street, the strip the Platt family lives on, is mysteriously transported through time and space to a place where dinosaurs still roam.

Devastation reigns as the dinosaurs destroy everything and everyone on the street, leaving the Platt family (and their cattle dog) trying to survive while also discovering where they are and how it happened.

The End of Oak Street is a movie the world needed.

Off the back of serious epic dramas like The Odyssey and the Marvel juggernaut that is Spider-Man, the cinema needed a real easy-going palate cleanser that is fun to watch but not three hours long.

We get both of those things here. An original story with eye candy, all while being under two hours long.

While not necessarily a family movie, it is one that will no doubt please crowds. When making a movie like this, there are a couple of must-haves: make it interesting and make it visually fun.

The premise ticks the first box.

For a majority of the runtime, there is little to no insight into what has actually happened.

It means that, as the audience, you are immersed in the world before you start to ask questions about it. Instead of asking how an entire street has been teleported and why it is happening, you are blown away by the fact that a T-Rex is snatching people up and eating them.

It goes for novelty over answers, and that’s what a movie about dinosaurs needs!

Second, it looks fantastic. An $80 million budget is nothing to sneeze at, but it is well below some of the ballooned costs of other mid-year blockbusters. It makes it all the more impressive that it looks better than most of those other films.

To put it into perspective, Jurassic World Rebirth, which was released last year, cost an estimated $180-225 million and looks about on par with what’s on show here.

The cast also completely understood what they were there to film.

McGregor is always great in everything he does, while Anne Hathaway continues her fantastic 2026 with her fourth film of the year, and another’s on the way.

By no means are they winning any awards, but they were having as much fun acting as I was watching, which is only a good thing.

The End of Oak Street won’t be crushing box office records, especially with other films performing the way that they are, but it does have the potential of being a classic that families will rewatch for years to come.

The End of Oak Street is currently showing in cinemas across the country.

canberra.title: School pitch to state policy: How Canberra students helped change the conversation on period poverty
canberra.snippet: When six Canberra High School students stood up at an International Women’s Day conference in 2021 to talk about period poverty, th...
canberra.content:
ACT government to install machines to dispense pads in schools across ACT. Photo: ACT government.

When six Canberra High School students stood up at an International Women’s Day conference in 2021 to talk about period poverty, they weren’t trying to change government policy.

They simply wanted to solve a problem many girls at their own school faced every month.

Five years later, their idea has helped make the ACT the first jurisdiction in Australia to legislate access to free period products for students, with dispenser machines now being installed in every public school across the Territory.

More than 90 of the ACT’s 93 public schools have already received the dispensers, with the remaining schools expected to be fitted out over the next three weeks.

Following a successful pilot in 31 public schools, the ACT Government is now installing free period product dispensers across every public school in the Territory.

Pads will be available through dispensers in primary schools, while high schools, P–10 schools and colleges will stock both pads and tampons. Period products will also continue to be available through school front offices.

The rollout forms part of the Period Products and Facilities (Access) Act 2023, making the ACT the first Australian jurisdiction to introduce legislation guaranteeing students access to free period products at school.

One of the students behind the original campaign, Amelia Tattam, said seeing the idea become reality was “beyond words”.

The campaign began when Amelia and five classmates represented Canberra High School at an International Women’s Day conference, joining students from 18 schools to develop solutions to issues affecting women and girls.

The group chose to tackle period poverty. At first, Amelia wasn’t sure how comfortable other students would be discussing the issue.

“There’s a lot of stigma around this issue,” she told Region.

“I found that a lot of students, in particular, tend to keep issues like this quiet. But once we started talking about it, a bunch of people came to us sharing their stories and telling us their experiences.

“We were really surprised that it was such an issue in our own school.”

The six students’ proposal won the conference pitch, paving the way for a trial of free pad and tampon dispensers at Canberra High School. The results exceeded their expectations.

There teacher Laura Gibbs who spearheaded the project said she is really proud public education teacher. “And even at our school, I wasn’t aware of the level of period poverty that we had here. So that was really valuable for me to realise that there were students in high school that were struggling to come to school because they didn’t have access to products,” she added.

Before the trial, 32 per cent of surveyed students said they had missed at least one day of school because they could not access period products. By the end of the trial, that figure had fallen to 3.3 per cent.

The project also helped break down the stigma surrounding menstruation.

Before the trial, only 25.1 per cent of students said they felt comfortable talking about periods with their peers. By the end, that had risen to 57 per cent.

“I think these figures really do go to show just how beneficial access is to these products, as well as improved education surrounding periods,” Amelia said.

“I am so very proud to see how effective the trial has been, not only in our own school but now across the whole ACT.”

Those results became the foundation for broader reform.

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said feedback from the pilot demonstrated the importance of allowing students to access period products privately and with dignity.

“We know from the trial that students have been able to get the pads and tampons they need freely and privately, with dignity and confidence, and in a way that helps them fully engage with their education and school life,” she said.

The minister also acknowledged the role played by the six former Canberra High School students and their teacher, Laura Gibbs.

“Their advocacy directly inspired the ACT Government’s nation-leading legislation and informed the wider rollout in ACT public schools.”

Women’s Minister Caitlin Tough said extending the program to primary schools was equally important, noting many girls begin menstruating before they reach high school.

“I got my first period in primary school, and so many of my friends did too,” she said.

“It’s a really awkward time when you’re in the upper years of primary school and your body’s changing.

“There’s no point waiting until high school. People’s bodies start changing while you’re still in primary school. We need to break that stigma and have those products available and just make them a normal part of everyday life.”

For Amelia, the ACT’s achievement should be just the beginning.

“I think 100 per cent expansion is the way to go because it’s very clear that this has been so effective within the ACT,” she said.

What started as an idea from six schoolgirls determined to solve a problem in their own classrooms has grown into a reform that will benefit thousands of students across the Territory — and, they hope, inspire other states to follow.

canberra.title: What are Ooshies worth? Well, it’s not nothing
canberra.snippet: We need to talk about Ooshies. I know, I know. We’re exhausted with the little buggers. Noticeboards are littered with posts about ...
canberra.content:
For every $30 spent, customers receive one of 40 unique characters. Some are “rarer” than others, and Ooshies have developed an economy of their own. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

We need to talk about Ooshies.

I know, I know. We’re exhausted with the little buggers. Noticeboards are littered with posts about these collectible figurines as people try to swap, buy or sell to complete their set. And with reports that “rare” specimens are selling for a small fortune, posters are sharing photos of specific Ooshies to question their worth.

Well, they’re not worth anything – but they’re not free.

Before diving deeper, it’s important to note that I have a small tribe in my house. They slipped surreptitiously into our lives one fateful day and instantly became a high-value item, according to my children.

For me, looking into their beady little eyes (the Oozies, not my children), I see my old Pizza Hut Land Before Time hand puppets looking back at me, and hear the faint clacking of Tazo against Tazo.

In marketing, incorporating a “surprise and delight” into your sales strategy is nothing new. Neither is producing “collectibles” or leveraging off a sense of scarcity with words like “rare”.

However, this is no longer cloak-and-dagger stuff. We grew up bombarded by advertising. We know its MO. We’re aware of marketing maneuvers and savvy at spotting sales tactics.

We also have more and more regulations in response to advancing research to keep advertising socially responsible.

We know that smoking kills, gambling is addictive – and microplastics live forever.

So how, in this day and age, are we still allowing ourselves to be bamboozled by this literal garbage?

First appearing in 2020, the original Ooshies promotion was an immediate hit, ending almost a month earlier than planned due to “unprecedented demand”.

Six years later – and 15 seconds closer to midnight on the Doomsday Clock – Woolworths says the new Ooshies are made from 97 per cent recycled materials.

We can only assume the remaining 3 per cent is made of pure whimsy.

Of course, this sounds like progress – which should never be discouraged – but let’s not pretend it’s a happy ending.

Given the scale of operations, what is the total carbon footprint of this new Ooshie population?

From raw material to production, packaging to transport, these cute little characters have quite a lifespan before they reach our shopping bags. And it all requires resources.

Also, “recyclable” doesn’t mean “recycled”.

Bins will be made available at Woolworths stores so we can “return any unused OOSHIES from the new range to Woolworths stores for recycling until 31 October 2026”.

No prizes for guessing whether people will be as motivated to return to the store to return their Ooshies as they were to acquire them. I suspect that ratio won’t exactly break even.

Not to mention the deadline. Or the further resources presumably required to re-process the little suckers into deck chairs, flooring, or some new “freebie” for the masses.

I’m not generally a fierce campaigner for the common person having the power to save the entire planet by switching to paper straws, but this? This is next level.

This entirely avoidable, utterly frivolous churning of resources is, frankly, a piss-take.

In 2026, as human-made junk surrounds us – floating through outer space and the depths of the Mariana Trench – how are we convinced that a piece of rubber is “rare”?

I won’t even touch on the “ultra-rare” Flocked Bullseye Ooshie allegedly marked as sold on eBay for millions. To dissect that situation, I’d need my tin foil hat.

So, for those asking “How much is this Ooshie worth?” and those answering: “Nothing”, well, that’s not quite true.

Lastly, adding to this value calculation, we must always remember: “If you’re not paying for the product, you are the product.”

With freebies and rewards programs, retailers buy our patronage, our data, our word-of-mouth.

And they play on our devotion to our children to do it – which I really resent. Adults make the purchasing decisions, so why aren’t these rewards aimed at us?

Well, of course, they are. Ooshies bring smiles to our children’s faces. They incentivise good behaviour at the shops and keep kids occupied once home. Practicalities aside, we’re also suckers for helping kids achieve a goal – hence the desperate pleas across social media from parents who “need help to complete our set”.

But you know what really shows devotion to our children? Safeguarding their future.

It really is that simple.

Parenting, at its core, is a series of tough decisions, boundaries and hard lines we hold to protect our children’s futures.

Why do we forget this when our kids come home begging for acid-filled squishies, ugly little dolls with dental problems, and other trendy crap?

So, there it is. That’s the cost. That’s how much your Ooshie is worth.

The unknown but inevitable environmental impact, and your service as a customer, a data point, and a peer-to-peer advertising machine.

All of undeniable value.

But then again, you never know. Maybe you’ll get one that’s worth millions on eBay.

canberra.title: The Spanish Australian Club’s monthly food market day is one of Canberra’s most charming ways to spend a Sunday
canberra.snippet: Located in Narrabundah, the Spanish Australian Club hosts a market day one Sunday a month built around three very good reasons to visit: ...
canberra.content:
It takes two people to carry the enormous seafood paella pan into the room. Photo: Sophia Brady.

Located in Narrabundah, the Spanish Australian Club hosts a market day one Sunday a month built around three very good reasons to visit: churros and hot chocolate for breakfast, a deli stocked with authentic Spanish ingredients and, to cap it all off, paella for lunch.

I arrived for breakfast, spent the morning shopping, went home to unpack my haul, and then returned for lunch because who can resist paella?

There is something familiar about the club. Even though I had never visited before, the building felt instantly recognisable.

Celebrating its 60th anniversary this year, the venue is, like many of Canberra’s older multicultural venues, very much a product of its era.

Rooms lead off in different directions from a central bar. There is a dance floor and a stage in the main hall, and I found myself picturing the place full of the founding community.

Today it is well maintained and spotless. The only thing that jars is the sporadic burst of noise from the small poker machine corner.

Breakfast is ordered from a small table beside the bar. You place your order, and someone disappears through a set of doors to cook the churros fresh because they are best enjoyed piping hot. Four pretty little golden pieces of fried dough, shaped like horseshoes, arrive with a cup of hot chocolate. Sugar and cinnamon sugar are there for dusting. We happily dunk and crunch next to the foosball table, which is attracting a lot of attention from the throng of young kids that morning.

Churros and hot chocolate for breakfast is a good reason to visit the monthly market. Photo: Sophia Brady.

While breakfast is underway, shoppers browse the deli. Fresh small goods sit on a table in the dining hall, while a small room behind is packed with pantry staples. Chorizo, morcilla, cheese, jamón, canned fish, beans, rice and spices are among the tempting options.

I was trying to decide what to buy when other shoppers started helpfully offering recommendations.

One woman pointed me towards the famed brand Cuca for my tinned fish selection and provided guidance on rice for paella. Others translated labels and explained some uses of products unfamiliar to me. I added a spicy paprika to my collection and bought bottles of traditional Asturian apple cider that I had not seen for sale in Canberra before.

The afternoon sees paella service start at 1 pm. You take a seat, and it all comes to you. First bread, then a nicely dressed bowl of salad, and finally the paella itself.

At the end of the meal, someone comes around to take payment. It takes two people to carry the enormous seafood paella pan into the room. It is very attractively presented and smells amazing. A vegetarian option is also available.

The seafood version included calamari, chicken, and a whole prawn crowning the rice. It was a good, honest and generous dish. Looking around the rooms, I saw literally every person eating it. It wasn’t just the guests at the tables; the volunteers in the serving area and the bar staff were all sharing the same meal.

Talk about communal dining! It was all very charming.

Paella lunch. Photo: Sophia Brady

While breakfast had attracted plenty of young families, lunch brought together many older members of the Spanish community. At the next table, a group of Spanish grandmothers shared a bottle of tempranillo and included us in a round of salud, the traditional toast to good health. We joined in before washing lunch down with a glass of tempranillo and an Estrella beer.

The paella costs $20 for guests and $15 for members. Membership costs $5. The maths to me was simple, so I became a member. Any leftover paella is packed up and sold as $10 takeaway. There were lots of takers, including me.

The Spanish Australian Club is located at 5 Narupai St, Narrabundah. The next market is on Sunday, 15 September, and then the first Sunday of the month for the rest of the year. Breakfast is served from 8 am to 10:30 am. The corner deli operates from 8 am to 11:30 am, and paella is served at 1 pm.

canberra.title: Public servant turns ‘relaxing and meditative’ pottery practice into side hustle
canberra.snippet: A surprise discovery has led a Canberra public servant to find much more than creativity in her side hustle. Public servant and ceramicis...
canberra.content:
16 August 2026

Start the conversation

Flynne Tytherleigh balances finance policy work with creativity. Photos: Flynne Tytherleigh.

A surprise discovery has led a Canberra public servant to find much more than creativity in her side hustle.

Public servant and ceramicist Flynne Tytherleigh is the first to say her two jobs are very different.

“I like being able to work my brain 9 am to 5 pm and work my hands 5 pm to 9 pm,” she says.

“I think it’s good to have a bit of a creative outlet.”

Flynne began throwing pottery as a therapeutic way of managing her endometriosis.

“Honestly, it started as a side hustle … Pottery was just a way of helping me to manage endometriosis pain.

“In hindsight, I had been seeing doctors and going and going to a pelvic physio … [It reached the point of] asking, ‘Do I try to get cannabis gummies or do I get a pottery wheel?’

“They were both around the same price.”

Flynne jokes her love of buying new glazes hasn’t meant it’s taken over her whole house – yet.

While she jokes her practice mugs mean her “gift cupboard is pretty good”, a strong reception to her early creations kept her going.

And it soon translated into an increasing number of online sales.

“It was very much friends and family and friends of friends, or people who had referred people to me,” she said of early purchases from her store.

“Then, one random Tuesday in June, it took off.”

Now, she’s kept busy with regular drops of about 10 mugs each week, custom projects (including repairs to sentimental mugs) and filling larger-scale orders for local businesses.

Most of her designs bear brightly coloured glazes and lower-case cheeky messages about our work life – think the Sunday scaries or the memes you text your mates.

Flynne’s designs – with sold-out designs like ‘good morning but at what cost?’ and ‘(completely overwhelmed) will do!!!’ – represent workplace stress.

“It is quite organic,” she says when asked how she comes up with a design.

“I’m thinking about what’s funny … What’s zeitgeist-y or popular on the internet, playing with trends.”

Cheese (the Chief Packing Officer) keeps a careful eye on your mugs. Photo: Flynne Tytherleigh.

Flynne splits her time between the public service and her pottery shop, after dropping back to four days a week in the office before the shop’s launch.

Beyond finding a creative outlet, she says it’s given her a way to de-stress.

“It can be physically demanding if you’re carrying clay up the stairs. I’m lucky that I’ve been able to turn something that I enjoy and find quite relaxing and meditative into a business – even if it was by accident.”

The support she’s received from her colleagues, customers and local businesses alike has left her “pinching herself”.

She says a major learning from launching her studio has been how it’s helped her embrace different parts of her personality.

“That’s just as important a part of your life as what you spend 40 hours per week on,” she says of our creative pursuits.

“You’re not just one person at home and one person at work … All those aspects of who you are are important.”

Follow the drops (or place your own order) on Flynne’s website.

australia.title: Japan’s defence minister heads to Australia to meet Marles in wake of melon-gate controversy
australia.snippet: Discussions to focus on Australia’s acquisition of Mogami-class frigates as Japan plays down Albanese’s podcast comments Japan’s defence ...
australia.content:
Japan’s defence minister will visit Canberra this week, the highest level engagement with Australia after controversy over Anthony Albanese’s comments about a gift of melons from prime minister Sanae Takaichi.

The defence minister, Shinjiro Koizumi, will meet his counterpart and deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on Tuesday, with discussions focused on Australia’s acquisition of Japan’s Mogami-class frigates and enhanced security cooperation.

Koizumi is considered a potential future prime minister of Japan. His father, Junichiro Koizumi, was prime minister from 2001 to 2006.

Koizumi’s visit comes after a week in which Albanese defended himself over comments made on the Bush Deep podcast, released last month.

He was discussing a pair of Japanese melons presented by Takaichi during a visit to Canberra earlier this year, and, while appearing to make hand gestures in front of his chest, said “she brought two, as you do”.

Host Nikki Osborne joked: “She came in looking like Pamela Anderson.”

Facing days of criticism from the opposition and in the media, Albanese has insisted his hand gestures and a comment about melons were misinterpreted and were not innuendo about breasts.

The opposition criticised Albanese for putting at risk close relations with one of Australia’s most important partners in Asia.

Public comments from Japan’s ambassador to Australia on Wednesday suggested Takaichi’s government wanted to avoid a diplomatic incident over the comments, which were initially not controversial but soon sparked strong criticism, including by a former envoy to Australia.

Japan’s government refrained from public comments on the issue until Wednesday, when its current ambassador to Australia Kazuhiro Suzuki released a statement not raising any further issue with Albanese’s conduct.

Suzuki noted Takaichi had visited Australia in May – shortly before the interview in question – and had been hosted for dinner by Albanese “in a very relaxed atmosphere, and we believe it helped build a personal trust relationship between the two leaders”.

Albanese had earlier apologised for comments about Australian signer Kylie Minogue made in the same appearance.

A Japanese diplomatic cable sent in July, and leaked during the controversy, blamed “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” and said Tokyo believed there was no “ill intention” in Albanese’s actions.

The visit comes as part of a five-day trip which will include a stop in India.

“Our relationship with Japan continues to go from strength to strength, and I look forward to welcoming my good friend, minister Koizumi back to Australia this week,” Marles told Guardian Australia.

“Together we will progress efforts to enhance defence cooperation and support our shared commitment to regional security, building on the joint statement announced by our prime ministers in May.

“This includes in the areas of co-developing and co-producing defence capabilities, advanced weapons testing, enhanced training and exercises, and increased information and intelligence cooperation.”

Takaichi has faced mounting political challenges, including on policies to help with the cost of living, and has seen sliding support in opinion polls in recent months.

Koizumi was criticised by China at the weekend for visiting the Yasukuni Shrine, dedicated to Japan’s war dead. Visits to the shrine by senior politicians are regularly criticised by Japan’s neighbours including China and South Korea, who suggest they are symbolic of a lack of remorse for Japan’s actions during the second world war.

In August last year, Labor agreed to buy Japan’s Mogami‑class frigates for the Royal Australian Navy.

Australia will spend $10bn over a decade to buy three of the frigates, with the first expected to be delivered in December 2029.

australia.title: Chalmers rejects Hanson’s call for more super access saying One Nation ‘wants to destroy’ scheme – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Anthony Albanese has just been speaking alongside th...
australia.content:
Key events

  • 4h ago

    What we learned, Sunday 16 August

  • 5h ago

    Disability advocacy organisations say NDIS reforms should not pass parliament

  • 5h ago

    Chalmers rejects Hanson's calls on superannuation

  • 8h ago

    Erin Patterson's appeal to begin in Melbourne on Wednesday

  • 8h ago

    Albanese says states 'have a willing partner' in commonwealth as NSW gun buyback announced

  • 9h ago

    Hanson says Australians should be able to use super for cost-of-living pressures

  • 9h ago

    Defence minister headed to PNG and Solomon Islands

  • 10h ago

    Hanson opposes gun buyback

  • 10h ago

    Welcome

What we learned, Sunday 16 August

And with that, we are going to close the blog. Before we go, let’s recap the big headlines:

  • An agreement was struck on a major federal-state gun buyback in response to the Bondi terror attack.

  • Triple murderer Erin Patterson’s appeal following her conviction for killing three relatives with poisoned beef wellingtons will begin in a Victorian court this week. Patterson was sentenced in September to life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 33 years for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt, Heather Wilkinson.

  • NDIS minister Jenny McAllister said a deal between the government and the Coalition to pass the reform was getting close.

  • Pauline Hanson said compulsory superannuation rules are too rigid in Australia and called for people under financial pressure or trying to buy their first home to get access to their retirement savings.

  • The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said Hanson was a threat to Australians’ retirement savings, warning her calls to loosen the rules for compulsory superannuation would hurt the system.

  • The Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, will visit Australia this week. Anutin will meet Anthony Albanese in Canberra on Wednesday to discuss deepening economic cooperation.

Thank you for spending part of your day with us. We will be back tomorrow with the blog.

Disability advocacy organisations say NDIS reforms should not pass parliament

A bit more from the NDIS minister, Jenny McAllister, who earlier said a deal between the government and the Coalition to pass the changes was getting close.

“We’re really hopeful and I’d go as far as saying confident that we can reach an agreement,” she told ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday.

The opposition health spokesperson, Anne Ruston, called for a strengthened fraud and corruption response within the disability insurance agency in the inquiry report.

McAllister said the government was still considering evidence brought forward during the inquiry process and flagged fraud as an area to work through with the Coalition.

But concerns about the changes remain among advocates – and from at least one state.

In a joint statement, 12 disability advocacy organisations said the reforms should not pass parliament in their current form.

The statement read:

Reform must be genuine and well-sequenced.

It must guarantee that people are not diverted from, or lose, NDIS supports unless alternative supports are funded, operational, accessible and available in practice.

Chalmers rejects Hanson's calls on superannuation

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson is a threat to Australian’s retirement savings, warning her calls to loosen the rules for compulsory superannuation would hurt the system.

Chalmers used a post on social media to pushback on Hanson’s comments this morning on News24, formerly Sky.

“One Nation wants to destroy the compulsory superannuation system, just like the Liberals and the Nationals,” Chalmers wrote.

They are all a threat to the retirement incomes and economic security of Australian workers.

Chalmers said Labor would defend the $4.5tn system.

Victoria Liberals to promise $50 a week road toll cap

Victorians would pay just $50 a week under a plan announced by Jess Wilson’s Liberal and Nationals team for two years from 1 July 2027.

The toll cap will apply to cars, light commercial vehicles and small business fleets of up to five vehicles.

Opposition leader and shadow treasurer, Jess Wilson, said:

Our toll cap will cut costs for families, tradies and small businesses and boost our economy.

By capping tolls for two years, a Liberal and Nationals Government will boost our economy and ensure families have more money to put towards the things that really matter.

Our $50 a week toll cap is part of my team’s Ten Year Economic Plan to lower costs, grow our economy and make Victoria the best place in the nation to do business.”

Erin Patterson's appeal to begin in Melbourne on Wednesday

Ben Smee

Triple murderer Erin Patterson’s appeal against her conviction for killing three relatives with poisoned beef wellingtons will begin in a Victorian court this week.

Patterson was sentenced in September to life imprisonment with a non-parole period of 33 years for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt, Heather Wilkinson.

She was also convicted of attempting to murder Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the lunch after spending weeks in hospital.

Patterson was convicted in July after an 11-week trial in Morwell in regional Victoria.

She maintained her innocence during the trial, claiming that she had not meant to serve beef wellingtons laced with death cap mushrooms to her lunch guests in July 2023.

Patterson is not appealing against her sentence, but prosecutors will argue she should never receive parole, and that her sentence was “manifestly inadequate”.

The state’s appeal against Patterson’s sentence argues the sentencing judge “erred in finding that there was a ‘substantial chance’ the respondent would be held in solitary confinement”.

They say this assessment “infected” the judge’s assessment of Patterson’s future conditions in custody and his decision to fix a non-parole period.

The Victorian court of appeal will hear the case on Wednesday and Thursday.

NSW opposition leader says gun buyback scheme ‘rushed’

The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has accused the state government of rushing the buyback scheme and has called on Labor to answer seven questions.

In a statement, Sloane said the Minns government must urgently explain the total anticipated cost of the buyback and how much will be paid by NSW; how the compensation amounts were determined; whether compensation would also apply to ammunition and other accessories; how many firearms are expected to be surrendered; why NSW is proceeding ahead of a national agreement; what safeguards will protect businesses and licence holders from financial loss; and whether NSW police are adequately resourced to administer the scheme.

Sloane said:

The NSW Liberals have consistently supported practical reforms that improve public safety. We will also continue to hold Labor accountable and ensure its laws are workable, properly funded and do not unfairly punish law-abiding citizens.

The Government must correct course, engage genuinely with affected stakeholders and resolve these concerns before the buyback begins.

Albanese says states 'have a willing partner' in commonwealth as NSW gun buyback announced

Anthony Albanese has just been speaking alongside the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, about the state’s gun buyback scheme agreed in response to the Bondi terror attack.

The prime minister said:

Australians are quite rightly proud of our gun laws but the fact is there are more guns in Australia today than there were at the time of dealing with the Port Arthur gun buyback that occurred under the Howard government.

These arrangements are available to every state and territory, and this reform comes on top of previous reforms that have been undertaken by my government in partnership with states and territories in particular the first ever development of a national firearms register.

That’s absolutely critical. I’ll continue to work constructively with states and territories.

They will make their own decisions under our federation system. They are responsible. But what I would say and reiterate is that in the commonwealth they have a willing partner. We know this is universally supported in some quarters.

This is controversial and it will be opposed. But we’ve made a decision.

Hanson says Australians should be able to use super for cost-of-living pressures

Tom McIlroy

The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, says compulsory superannuation rules are too rigid in Australia and called for people under financial pressure or trying to buy their first home to get access to their retirement savings.

“A lot of Australians are doing it tough now and struggling to pay off their mortgages,” Hanson told News24.

In some ways, I feel that you should give them their money now, and let them help them with the cost of living.

It is their money; they’ve they’ve sacrificed it in lieu of pay. So, in a lot of cases, people want it.

She called for the rules to be “lightened up a bit” so workers can use their money in times of crisis.

“It is their money,” Hanson said.

‘Additional arrangements’ being worked on for children removed from NDIS, minister says

Asked what happens to a nine-year-old who is removed from the NDIS, McAllister said:

We will need to work through the additional Foundational Supports.

There’s $10bn that premiers and the prime minister have agreed ought to be applied to standing up Foundational Supports.

We started with children, but we know that we’ll need to stand up … and make additional arrangements.

NDIS minister says Thriving Kids scheme on track to commence from 1 October

The minister for disability and the NDIS, Jenny McAllister, has been on Insiders, where she was asked about Thriving Kids, which states and territories will start rolling out on 1 October.

She said:

We are, in every other state, seeing the states getting moving, and I’m really confident – having met with state and territory counterparts on Friday – that we will see these states ready to move.

Defence minister headed to PNG and Solomon Islands

Tom McIlroy

Richard Marles is visiting Port Moresby and Honiara this weekend, meeting with Papua New Guinea’s prime minister, James Marape, and defence minister, Elias Kapavore, today.

Discussions will focus on strengthening defence cooperation and advancing implementation of the historic Pukpuk treaty.

Marles will then head to Solomon Islands and meet with the country’s prime minister, Matthew Wale, and join government ministers at the opening of the Western Border Outpost in the Shortland Islands.

The facility will bring together police, customs, immigration and biosecurity officials in one location, and support Solomon Islands’ Guardian-class patrol boats.

“Pacific security is most effective when it is led by Pacific nations,” Marles said.

Australia is proud to work alongside our Pacific partners to support their priorities and contribute to a secure, stable and resilient region.

Tom McIlroy

‘I don’t like the gay Mardi Gras’: Hanson

Pauline Hanson has renewed her criticism of the Sydney gay and lesbian Mardi Gras, saying she doesn’t like the annual event.

Back in her first stint in federal politics, Hanson told journalist Tracey Curro that she believed the event promoted something that is “unnatural”.

On Sunday, she said gay marriage was legal in Australia, describing it as “acceptable”.

“I still don’t like the gay Mardi Gras, but that’s my opinion,” she said.

I think your own personal sexuality should be kept in closed doors, behind closed doors. It’s no one’s business to do it out there with the gay Mardi Gras anywhere.

I know it brings a lot of tourists to the country. I know it brings a lot of money. I know all this, but that’s my personal opinion. But anyway, good luck to them that they want to do that.

The comments come after One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce claimed the party was one of “the gayest” in federal politics last week.

Sydney’s Mardi Gras has been going since 1978. Starting as a gay rights protest, marking the anniversary of New York’s Stonewall uprising, the parade was a protest against homophobia and police brutality.

Some history here:

Tom McIlroy

Thai prime minister to visit Canberra

Anthony Albanese says his Thai counterpart, Anutin Charnvirakul, will visit Australia this week.

The two leaders will meet in Canberra on Wednesday to discuss deepening economic cooperation.

The visit will be Prime Minister Anutin’s first to Australia since taking office. Albanese said:

Australia and Thailand enjoy a warm relationship, built on trust and a shared commitment to a prosperous Indo-Pacific.

Many Australians have experienced Thailand’s warmth and hospitality through travel, while the Thai-Australian community continues to enrich our nation and strengthen the enduring ties between our countries through business and culture.

Tom McIlroy

Hanson wants to slash international student numbers

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says she wants dramatic cuts to the number of international students allowed to come into the country.

Hanson is refusing to say how much overseas migration should be cut, but agrees with News24 host Andrew Clennell that she wants to slash overseas student numbers.

“I think the international student industry that’s been set up by the universities is a farce,” she said.

People are using it to come to the country. Then after they get in the country, they’re only here for a few months. Then they change the courses.

Then they apply for residence here in Australia. So they’re using [it] as a back door to get into the country.

Hanson opposes gun buyback

Tom McIlroy

Pauline Hanson says she is opposed to a major gun buyback being announced by Anthony Albanese and the NSW premier, Chris Minns, in Sydney shortly.

Legislation for the plan passed parliament earlier this year, part of the response to the Bondi beach terror attack. It will be run in two phases, with the cost split 50:50 between the federal and NSW governments.

Under the first phase of the scheme, $1,000 will be paid for revolvers and $850 for semi-automatic handguns. Compensation of $850 will be paid for double-barrel shotguns and $650 for those with a single barrel.

Between $650 and $1,000 will be paid for rifles, while air rifles have a fixed compensation of $450.

Hanson told News24 taxpayers should not pay for the scheme.

She suggested the buyback would impact “law-abiding Australians who are trying to go about their business, like farmers that need their guns,” she said.

A different gun is for a different purpose, and you have to understand guns. I’ve got my own gun licence, so I understand these people.

Welcome

Good morning.

There is a bit of news around today. An agreement has been struck on a major federal-state gun buyback in response to the Bondi terror attack.

The commonwealth and NSW governments will evenly share the cost of the scheme.

National cabinet agreed to fight antisemitism and strengthen firearms restrictions across the nation after the deadly December 2025 shooting.

We’re expecting to hear from the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and NSW premier, Chris Minns, soon.

And in other news, a little penguin has died from bird flu before a vaccination program begins, amid new positive detections of the deadly virus in wild birds across two states.

Victorian authorities confirmed the death of a penguin from Phillip Island on Saturday afternoon, the first detection in a penguin in the state.

Let’s get into today’s news.

australia.title: NSW to begin Australia’s biggest gun buyback in decades in wake of Bondi terror attack
australia.snippet: Albanese and Minns said buyback would begin in two phases from 2 November, with state and commonwealth to split costs Follow our Australi...
australia.content:
New South Wales will become the first state to undertake Australia’s biggest gun buyback in 30 years in a jointly funded scheme in response to the Bondi beach terror attack.

Anthony Albanese and the Minns government said the buyback would begin in two phases from 2 November.

Under the first phase, $1,000 will be paid for revolvers and $850 for semi-automatic handguns.

Compensation of $850 will be paid for double-barrel shotguns and $650 for those with a single barrel.

Between $650 and $1,000 will be paid for rifles, while air rifles have a fixed compensation of $450.

“We must do everything we can to make sure the antisemitic terrorist attack in Bondi doesn’t happen again. That includes meaningful nationwide gun reform,” the prime minister said.

The federal and NSW governments said phase 2 would begin in early 2027, and provide “a pathway to compensation” for “eligible higher-value firearms with an indicative market value above $3,000, capped at $10,000 per firearm”.

The federal government announced the buyback scheme in the wake of the deadly terrorist attack at Sydney’s Bondi beach on 14 December 2025, in which two gunmen shot dead 15 people.

NSW also tightened the state’s gun laws in response to the shooting. The laws restrict the number of guns an individual can own to four, with exceptions for farmers and professional shooters, who are restricted to 10.

The laws also reclassified some weapons – including banning firearms that allow multiple shots without reloading.

NSW police will administer the state’s buyback, which will compensate individuals for surrendering firearms that exceed the new ownership limits or which have been reclassified.

A government spokesperson said the commonwealth would contribute 50% for administration costs, and fully fund the destruction costs for surrendered firearms and administration.

Buyback to happen in phases

Phase 1 would also include an “initial industry support package” for businesses and dealers, including grants of up to $25,000 and one-off licence fee relief “worth $500 over two years per dealer”.

Phase 2 would also include further industry support with details to be announced at a later date, the government said.

“After Bondi, we promised the people of New South Wales we would introduce the toughest gun laws in the country, and that’s exactly what we did,” said the state’s premier, Chris Minns.

The NSW government estimates up to 274,000 registered firearms – approximately 24% of the total number of registered guns in the state – will be affected by the new limits.

“There are potentially hundreds of thousands of firearms affected by these changes. We want those guns handed in, compensated for and safely destroyed,” Minns said.

‘Legitimate concerns’

The state’s opposition leader, Kelly Sloane, said the government must still address “legitimate concerns” about the buyback urgently, before it comes into effect.

Sloane said the buyback had been promoted as a national scheme, but that other jurisdictions had refused to participate. She also questioned the cost.

“The fixed payments announced for most firearms do not reflect their individual market value,” Sloane said.

“While the Commonwealth and NSW have agreed to share the acquisition costs, the Government has not disclosed the scheme’s total anticipated cost or identified the [budget] allocation that will fund it.

“The government says it will provide a flat payment for associated ammunition but has failed to disclose the amount, eligibility criteria or whether affected accessories and other property rendered unusable by its laws will be compensated.”

The broader national plan has run into opposition from several states and faces a fresh challenge in federal parliament.

The Nationals have tabled a bill in the Senate to repeal Labor’s federal firearms crackdown and abolish the proposed national buyback.

Leader Matt Canavan called the reforms a “kneejerk and unnecessary piece of legislation that was never properly consulted on” as the rural party accused the government of unfairly targeting law-abiding gun owners.

Those concerns were echoed by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who insisted the Bondi attack was the result of individual bad actors.

“It wasn’t the guns,” she told News24 on Sunday.

“It was the people behind the guns that are responsible for the Bondi massacre.”

The deal with NSW followed the Queensland and Victoria governments both rejecting the proposed buyback scheme. The Northern Territory said it won’t contribute any money for a buyback, while South Australia has not announced any progress since giving “in principle” support in January.

The ACT and Tasmania have agreed to the deal, but funding negotiations are ongoing.

Western Australia completed its own buybacks in January but has signalled willingness to participate in the federal scheme.

The move comes after the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion recommended that governments “prioritise efforts to finalise and implement an updated and nationally consistent national firearms agreement and the proposed buyback scheme”.

australia.title: ‘Systemic racism at work’: Sydney council plan for compulsory English shop signage condemned as ‘kind of crazy’
australia.snippet: Strathfield council plan ridiculed for making life harder for small business and failing to consult local communities Follow our Australi...
australia.content:
Along a bustling street in Sydney’s west, Asian grocers sit alongside Nepalese restaurants displaying images of the tantalising curries inside. Here, on one of Strathfield’s busiest commercial streets, a Nepalese grocer is nestled between a 7-Eleven and a medical clinic. Two doors down, a butcher run by the same owners welcomes customers with a sign that reads “Strathfield Veggie Shed” in Nepali.

Bilingual signs are common in Sydney’s west. It is a similar scene in other major cities, such as Melbourne’s Box Hill where almost 30% of residents were born in China and many shops signs include Chinese characters alongside English text.

But last month, Strathfield council passed a motion advocating that local shopfront signs “clearly and prominently” display English.

Vivek Shrestha, who has proudly displayed his Nepali sign at the front of the Strathfield Veggie Shed for the past four years and also owns the butcher shop, says he has already ordered a new sign to avoid future penalties by a council action he says is “unfair”.

“My customers – like 90% – [are] Nepalese,” he says. “I don’t think changing [the sign] to English is going to add on the customers.

“My product line is very basic and the target is … only the Nepalese customer.”

It’s unclear how the policy, which does not prevent other languages from being used but says English should be displayed “clearly and prominently”, will be enforced. A council spokesperson says no changes to signage requirements will be made until a planned report on any existing policies is considered.

But Australia’s race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, describes the move as an example of “systemic racism in operation”, and says he’s worried it could lead to similar moves by other councils.

“The way racism operates, particularly through laws and policies and procedures, is that it forces people – or in this case, businesses and the people that run them – to shed themselves of their identity, to diminish themselves,” he says.

“Language is a critical part of people’s identity,” he says.

Sivaraman points to a lack of consultation with the communities and businesses affected by Strathfield council’s move.

“Communities of colour, communities that are different, are simply told that they must do a particular thing as part of a process of assimilation, rather than being consulted,” he says.

The council’s spokesperson says community consultation will occur during the review of it’s policies.

But Strathfield Labor councillor Rory Nosworthy, who voted against the motion, says he isn’t aware of anyone complaining about signs.

“It’s not an issue I’ve observed or heard about,’ he said.

“The majority of stores already have partial English signage. It’s a bit of a non-issue,” he says.

A spokesperson for the Municipal Association of Victoria – the peak body for local government in that state – says it can’t recall any similar discussions from councils about the issue.

The federal opposition’s leader in the Senate, Michaelia Cash, went further. She told Channel 9 this week that small businesses did not need “another layer of council regulation” and stressed they “know their customers.”

Cultural diversity

In Strathfield – in which about 73% of households speak a non-English language at home – a similar idea was proposed eight years ago.

At the time, the council sought to make sure community languages were no bigger than 30% of the English signage. But the proposal attracted significant backlash.

In the early 2000s, a number of Sydney councils began to stipulate or encourage the use of English on shop signs.

In neighbouring Burwood, where a bustling multicultural food scene thrives, the council’s guidance for its street appeal shopfront improvement program stipulates information on language use.

“Signage to be mainly in English, can also be in an additional language,” it says. For awnings, it says English is to be the “prominent language.”

A spokesperson for Sydney’s Cumberland city council, where almost 74% of households speak a non-English language, says multilingual shop signs and storefronts contributed to “the unique character and identity” of the area.

The council’s development control plan states that advertising and signage “shall be displayed in English but may include a translation in another language”.

The Strathfield council decision comes amid a debate about multiculturalism and social cohesion on the political right in recent months.

Liberal councillor, Esther Kim, who put forward the motion, said she was motivated by an advertisement in a community language that she had seen plastered on the exterior of a toilet block in Carlingford. The suburb is in the neighbouring council of Parramatta.

“If one multicultural language is being used, only … that community understands it. All others [are] excluded,” Kim says.

“We have to be united with multiculturalism.”

Kim, who migrated to Australia almost 40 years ago from South Korea, says requiring English to be on shopfront signs would attract more diners to the area’s so-called Koreatown.

“We will bring more people here because they can understand what is going on here,” she says.

“If they want to use their language, you have to include English too.”

The council has not publicly released any information on how many shops within the LGA do not include English on their signs.

Some locals, like university student Olivia Toms, says the move is “kind of crazy”.

“English speakers are very much able to do research and easily translate the signs if they want to. There are options for that … I feel like I’m exposed to so many different cultures, languages and foods that I wouldn’t normally be exposed to.”

The 21-year-old says it’s unfair “for immigrants and small-business owners”.

“If it’s something the government is enforcing, they should be the ones paying for the signage, in my opinion,” she says.

australia.title: Could you save money on your mortgage? As house prices cool and lender rivalry heats up, experts say Australians should ask
australia.snippet: There is talk that lenders are starting to compete more fiercely for customers as demand for new home loans drops Follow our Australia ne...
australia.content:
Homeowners with a mortgage dodged a bullet this week when the Reserve Bank of Australia board chose to hold its official cash rate at 4.35%.

The reprieve may prove short-lived, though, with a number of economists and financial markets seeing a good chance of another hike this year.

That would add to the three RBA rate hikes earlier this year, which have all piled further pressure on indebted households already struggling with high cost of living.

The best defence, as they say, is offence. There is talk that lenders are starting to compete more fiercely for customers, including by offering better deals.

Let’s take a look at what’s happening, and how you could benefit.

world.title: Zimbabwe boat accident death toll hits 68 as 22 more bodies recovered
world.snippet: Eighteen children among the people killed after ferry capsized on Lake Kariba Twenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat acc...
world.content:
Twenty-two more bodies have been recovered after a boat accident in Zimbabwe, taking the death toll to 68, police said on Saturday.

The ferry capsized on Tuesday on Lake Kariba, on the border with Zambia. An investigation has suggested it was overloaded when it turned over during heavy winds.

Eighteen children were among the people killed, Zimbabwe’s police said, in what is believed to be the country’s deadliest such disaster.

Most of the passengers are believed to be villagers and fish traders who lived around the lake.

Officials said the vessel was authorised to carry 90 people but was packed with 114 adults, five crew members and an unspecified number of children.

Lt Col Joseph Muchechesi, commander of the boat regiment involved in the search operation, said: “So far today we have managed to take 22 bodies. We are confident that we will manage to retrieve all the bodies.”

The civil protection unit said on Wednesday that 77 people had been rescued.

Hundreds of people gathered at the district hospital in the lakeside town of Kariba to identify the bodies of their relatives and loved ones.

A public memorial service was held in Kariba, nearly 280km (175 miles) north-west of the capital Harare, on Thursday before the burials started.

Survivors said they pleaded with the ferry driver to turn back as the vessel had begun taking on water soon after departing.

Chance Siyamavhu, 45, told Agence France-Presse: “Thank God that a wave pushed the sinking vessel and we managed to climb on top.

“When the boat capsized, most of the people scrambled to get the lifejackets but most of them did not even know how to use them.

“Most people could not make it.”

Lake Kariba is the world’s largest manmade lake by volume. It stretches more than 200km (124 miles) and is up to 40km (25 miles) wide in places.

It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people.

In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.

On the Zimbabwean side, five passengers drowned in a 2021 incident.

world.title: Moroccan police arrest more than 100 people as they attempt to enter Ceuta
world.snippet: Border security tightened after social media posts call for another mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory Moroccan police ha...
world.content:
Moroccan police have arrested 111 people as they tried to enter Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, amid ⁠tightened security on both sides after social media posts ​called for another mass crossing.

The attempted crossing on Saturday came two weeks after more than 72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta, causing tensions within the EU and prompting anti-immigration rhetoric among far-right parties worldwide. At least 96 people died trying to ⁠reach European soil.

A source in Morocco’s interior ministry told news agency Reuters that those detained included 109 migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two Moroccan citizens arrested in or around Fnideq, the Moroccan city near Ceuta.

Moroccan police used teargas to disperse groups of migrants ⁠gathered on hills about 1.9 miles (3km) from the border, according to Spanish news agency EFE. Reuters later saw hundreds of police officers, some in riot gear and others in plainclothes, returning from the hills outside ​Fnideq.

EFE and Spanish state broadcaster TVE said Morocco’s interior ministry ordered their journalists ‌to leave Fnideq immediately, without providing an explanation.

In Ceuta, ‌Spanish soldiers guarded supermarkets while police patrolled the main streets. The city was calmer than in the days after the deadly crossing attempt on 30 July.

Madrid has ‌since installed a maritime barrier and deployed more than 500 additional police officers from mainland Spain, raising the total in Ceuta to more than 1,600. The interior ministry said the reinforcements would remain for as long as needed.

“We’ll continue to deploy whatever personnel are necessary to restore normality as soon as possible and prevent events like those of 30 July from happening again,” Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said on Thursday.

About 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta, the minister added. Reuters saw hundreds sheltering from scorching heat under makeshift bamboo shelters on the urban beach of El Trampolin.

Grande-Marlaska said migrants who entered irregularly would not be allowed to stay in the territory, travel to mainland Spain or ‌obtain legal status, except in rare cases involving extreme vulnerability. Those without a right to remain would be returned to Morocco, he added.

Earlier this week, Rabat said it was monitoring “the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin” calling for a mass crossing ​on 15 August, warning it would prosecute organisers and participants.

A Reuters witness saw reinforced security near the border, including police vans with wire shields and road checkpoints. Local media reported similar measures near Melilla, another Spanish territory in north Africa.

Authorities prevented several groups from boarding trains and buses to northern Morocco in cities such as Casablanca, Fez and Kenitra. However, witnesses told Reuters that some migrants from sub-Saharan Africa were bypassing security checkpoints by taking mountain routes towards Fnideq.

One witness said the schools in Fnideq had been turned into accommodation for security forces deployed near the ⁠border.

world.title: American missionary kidnapped in Niger freed after nine months
world.snippet: Kevin Rideout, who was abducted by unknown assailants in Niamey, said to be in good health and in care of US officials An American missio...
world.content:
An American missionary who was kidnapped in Niger in October has been released, his organisation has said.

Serving in Mission International said Kevin Rideout “is in good health in the care of US officials” and would soon be reunited with his extended family.

Donald Trump, who claimed to have helped secure Rideout’s release, later said he was “back in United States Custody” on Friday.

The 50-year-old missionary pilot was kidnapped in the west African country’s capital, Niamey, on 21 October by three armed individuals and was probably driven out of town, according to a security official at the time. No armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction. Other details about his rescue remain unknown.

The US president’s administration had made the release of Rideout a priority in its latest strategy on African Sahel states, after years of fighting extremism found limited success. Rideout had been working in Niger for 19 years as a missionary before the incident.

“I am proud to announce that Kevin Rideout, a wonderful Christian Missionary, is back in United States Custody,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Friday. “Kevin, the United States of America looks forward to welcoming you HOME. Glad to have helped!”

Niger has long been the target of attacks by armed groups, including jihadis linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State. A “continually deteriorating security situation” across the country was cited by the military junta that took power in 2023 when deposing the democratically elected president, Mohamed Bazoum.

The new authorities ousted western partners, including the US, which had soldiers in Niger, and forged a new security and diplomatic alliance with Russia. One former US base has since been occupied by Russian soldiers.

Trump described the broader region of west Africa as “the epicenter of Islamist terrorism” in his social media post on Friday, claiming there had been “more deadly attacks in the past year” there than anywhere else on Earth.

Washington has since shifted its focus to coastal west African states including Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, sharing intelligence with local security personnel to prevent extremist threats from spilling southwards from the arid Sahel.

However, the insurgency continues to escalate in the region. In Niger, data from Acled, the armed conflict data aggregator, shows that civilian fatalities rose by nearly 50% in the year after Bazoum was ousted.

Cities and urban centres in the Sahel region have also been increasingly targeted by armed non-state actors as the crisis reaches new dimensions.

The US embassy in Niamey issued a security alert a day after Rideout’s abduction, warning that American citizens “remain at a heightened risk of kidnapping throughout Niger, including in the capital city”.

In June, more than 30 people were killed when gunmen attacked the main airport in Niamey. It was the second attack this year at the airport, a strategic hub that serves as the ruling military’s command, hosting its air force base and most of its drones and aircraft. It is also the headquarters of the Alliance of Sahel States, the regional alliance that brings together troops from Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.

In April, Mali’s defence minister, Gen Sadio Camara, was killed in his home on the outskirts of the capital Bamako during coordinated assaults staged by insurgents including the west African affiliate of al-Qaida.

Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

world.title: DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province
world.snippet: Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever The Ebola outbreak in th...
world.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago.

The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data.

Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak.

The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded.

The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming that Ebola is not real.

Health workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months.

The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February.

Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate.

Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.”

Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”.

Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months.

Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time.

This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in a paper published this week in the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola.

Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the virus could be mutating and that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate.

Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story.

world.title: French ambassador to CAR investigated over claims he hosted dozens of women
world.snippet: Disciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residence France has opened disciplina...
world.content:
France has opened disciplinary proceedings against its ambassador to Central African Republic over allegations of misconduct, after claims he brought dozens of women into his official residence, raising potential security concerns.

The investigation comes as Paris seeks to rebuild relations with CAR after their sharp deterioration in recent years amid Russia’s expanding influence in the former French colony.

The French weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported that the ambassador, Bruno Foucher, 65, brought about 30 women between the ages of 20 and 30 into his residence during the period of January 2024 to March 2026, with some of them staying overnight. The visits prompted officials to report a security breach.

The ambassador acknowledged having had sexual relations with two young women, the weekly said.

The French foreign ministry said: “At the initiative of the ministry, an administrative investigation was carried out in Bangui in 2026. Upon receipt of the findings of this mission, and at the request of the minister, the ministry initiated disciplinary proceedings against the ambassador. These proceedings are ongoing.”

The ministry conducted an on-site inspection in April, which led to the opening of disciplinary proceedings.

Foucher is a career diplomat who has served as ambassador to CAR since 2023. He was ambassador to Lebanon from 2017 to 2020, to Iran from 2011 to 2016, and to Chad between 2006 and 2011.

According to Le Canard enchaîné, which said it obtained the inspection report, the ambassador received about 15 visits a month.

He also allegedly instructed staff to allow one of the young women to stay at the residence during his absence.

Russia maintains a strong foothold in CAR, primarily through the Wagner paramilitary group, which plays a key role in providing security for the country’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra.

French officials have accused Russians of fostering anti-French sentiment in a number of African countries.

The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, praised the “complete restoration of relations” between France and CAR when he visited Bangui in March.
